verses.text: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem:
“Vanity of vanities,” says the Preacher; “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.”
What does man gain from all his labor in which he labors under the sun?
One generation goes, and another generation comes; but the earth remains forever.
The sun also rises, and the sun goes down, and hurries to its place where it rises.
The wind goes toward the south, and turns around to the north. It turns around continually as it goes, and the wind returns again to its courses.
All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full. To the place where the rivers flow, there they flow again.
All things are full of weariness beyond uttering. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
That which has been is that which shall be; and that which has been done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun.
Is there a thing of which it may be said, “Behold,  this is new?” It has been long ago, in the ages which were before us.
There is no memory of the former; neither shall there be any memory of the latter that are to come, among those that shall come after.
I, the Preacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom concerning all that is done under the sky. It is a heavy burden that God  has given to the sons of men to be afflicted with.
I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and behold, all is vanity and a chasing after wind.
That which is crooked can’t be made straight; and that which is lacking can’t be counted.
I said to myself, “Behold, I have obtained for myself great wisdom above all who were before me in Jerusalem. Yes, my heart has had great experience of wisdom and knowledge.”
I applied my heart to know wisdom, and to know madness and folly. I perceived that this also was a chasing after wind.
For in much wisdom is much grief; and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.

footnotes.content: Solomon speaks to us from his throne, and he is king over Israel in Jerusalem. Yet even a king who has seen everything will ask the deepest questions about life's meaning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Vanity of vanities"—he says it twice because the weight of it fills him. When a man chases only what he can see and hold, he finds his hands always empty. But Jesus offers us something that lasts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "What does man gain?" A good question to sit with. Our labor here is real and good, but it cannot be the final answer to our hunger for meaning. Christ alone fills that hunger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Generations come and go like waves, but the earth remains. There is comfort in that steadiness—God's creation outlasts our small seasons, and His hand stays sure through all of them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sun rises and sets in its ordained pattern. There is something both humbling and restful about that regularity—we do not have to keep the sun in its course. God's faithfulness works while we rest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wind's endless turning is an ancient way of saying: everything moves in circles. In Scripture, the wind often brings the breath of God. Yet even the Spirit's work in our hearts moves deeper than these visible cycles.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All rivers run to the sea, yet it never overflows—a picture of endless want. Our hearts are like that sea too, hungry for something no earthly stream will ever satisfy. Only Christ fills that deep place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "All things are full of weariness." He speaks plainly here about fatigue—of body, of eye, of ear. This is the tiredness that comes from seeking meaning without finding God. With Him, our labor finds its rest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nothing is truly new under the sun—history repeats, patterns recur. We think we invent, but we are walking paths others have walked. This should humble us and turn our eyes toward what is above the sun: the eternal God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Someone will claim they have found something new, but it was already old before we were born. We are not the first to feel what we feel, to dream what we dream. That loneliness we fear—others have felt it too, and Jesus knew it on the cross.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No one remembers the past; no one will remember us. This sounds like despair, but it is a gift: we are freed from the weight of making ourselves eternal. God remembers us. That is enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon establishes himself: I was king, I had power, I stood over Jerusalem. Yet he speaks of it as something past, something he reflects on. Even a king's throne is a vantage point from which to see how small all earthly crowns truly are.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He applied his heart to seek wisdom and found it a heavy burden. God allows us to see deeply, to ask hard questions—not to crush us, but so we will stop looking only at what is under the sun and lift our eyes to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "All is vanity and a chasing after wind." He has seen all the works done under the sun, and they are empty pursuit. Yet in that emptiness, he teaches us something merciful: stop chasing the wind. Turn to the One who stands still and calls us home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The crooked cannot be straightened; what lacks cannot be counted—he speaks of human limits, the things we cannot fix by our own strength. This was true in Solomon's day and in ours. Only Christ straightens the bent places in us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I have obtained great wisdom above all who were before me." Even a voice saying this—claiming to surpass all others—admits in the next breath that wisdom itself is wind. Pride speaks loud, but it is hollow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He sought to know both wisdom and madness, the high and the low. Yet he finds that chasing either one is still chasing wind—grasping at what slips through our fingers. True knowledge is knowing God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this: the more we know without Christ, the more we grieve. Yet with Him, our knowing becomes wisdom that carries joy beneath the sorrow. As we see Him more clearly, we understand both the weight and the grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
